newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Rain worries NW Europe cereals farmers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rain worries NW Europe cereals farmers.

text.p: Wet weather across north-western Europe is likely to mean delays to cereals harvesting and quality concerns.
Apart from Britain, northern France, Germany, the low countries and southern Scandinavia were affected by rain, a spokesman for the UK's Meteorological Office said.
"Generally speaking you could say that the areas which were worst affected by the drought, apart from Iberia, are the ones getting the rain," the spokesman said.
Rain and cold temperatures delayed the start of the field pea harvest in northern France while combining went on rapidly in the south, industry group UNIP said on Friday.
It said that as of June 25 the harvest was half complete in the southwest and southeast with initial results suggesting wide variations in yields depending on moisture levels.
But heading north, wet conditions prevented farmers from starting the harvest in the Poitou-Charentes and Pays-de-Loire regions.
In northern France colder temperatures sharply slowed down crop development but were not yet threatening yield potential.
But as more rain is forecast for the coming days, farmers fear that harvesting of crops that have reached maturity will be pushed back.

In Germany, changeable German crop weather with plenty of rain is making up for earlier moisture deficits as farmers prepare for the barley harvest from mid-July, a source at the meteorological office, DWD, said.
Harvests would be delayed by up to ten days because the spring was too cool for crops to develop quickly, and because they needed to dry off, he said.
"But it's not a problem for yields, rather one of rearranging labour schedules," he said.
Only the driest areas in the south of eastern Germany and in northern Bavaria might see some yield losses.
Grains, rapeseed and sugar beet were in good shape, with only maize needing warmer temperatures, DWD said.
In Britain, wet weather could hit the yield and quality achieved by the new cereals crop, traders and analysts said.
Concern over too much moisture follows months of worries over not enough, after the driest start to the year since 1929, was seen then as a threat to yields.
"If it keeps on like this it could be very bad," one farming source said. "If it stops raining today and gets sunny it could be a good one," he said.
By midnight on Wednesday the London Weather Centre had recorded 84 millimeters of rain so far in June, almost double the 45.4 millimeter average.

The most pressing problem is for barley, analysts said. Traders fear that the wet could cut quality and there is concern that much of the crop is laying down, because of the rain, making harvesting more difficult.

Wheat is mainly in the dull ripe stage. "If it goes on like this yields will be affected first and then Hagberg," an expert at the ADAS agricultural advisory service said, referring to the Hagberg measure of quality.
Even if the weather turns fine, soil moisture was well up, he said. This was likely to mean heavy dews for some time, he said.
Although northern countries have been worst hit, there are concerns in Spain.
Continual rain is delaying harvesting and prompting fears that wheat and barley crop quality and specific weights will be worsened, although it may yet be too early to determine the specific effect.

"It's not so much that there's been heavy rain, its just that it's been continual and so people start to worry about quality. Barley is more resistant than wheat, but still the weather has not really been good news," said a trader in the north of Spain.
--Christopher Lyddon, London newsroom +44 171 542 7928
